title: Promise Delivered: Welcome to the DEV Hall of Fame (65 Authors, 65 Masterpieces)
author: Giorgi Kobaidze
body:
*Status: Promise delivered ✅*

---

## The Doors Are Open

A little over a month ago, I published this:

{% embed https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/show-me-the-article-youre-most-proud-of-and-ill-read-every-single-one-of-them-1l53 %}

The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you *love* the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.

I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.

Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.

That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: **"Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"**

So here it is.

Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

> 📌 **A quick note:** A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

---

## Visitor Stats 📊

Before the tour starts, a few numbers:

- **65 authors, 65 masterpieces.**
- **600+ minutes** of listed reading time. That's over 10 hours, and in reality it was much more, because listed reading time is a polite lie.
- **The longest read:** 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100.
- **The shortest read:** 1 minute.
- **The oldest exhibit:** published in March 2020.
- **The most reactions:** 623.
- **Zero reactions:** 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists.

---

## How to Tour the Hall

The exhibits are grouped into wings by theme, so you can head straight to whatever interests you most. Each exhibit has the article itself, why the author picked it (when they told me), and my take.

- 🚪 **The Welcome Desk:** where every visitor should start
- 🏛️ **Stories From the Trenches:** careers, first steps, and the people behind the code
- 💡 **The "Finally, It Clicked" Gallery:** fundamentals explained the way they should be
- ⚙️ **The Engine Room:** systems, internals, and seriously deep dives
- 🤖 **The AI Lab:** building with AI, and finding out where it breaks
- 🧠 **The Philosophy Floor:** thinking about AI, engineering, and the craft itself
- 🔧 **The Builder's Garage:** real tools solving real problems

Grab a coffee. It's a big building.

---

## 🚪 The Welcome Desk

### [FrancisTRDev](https://dev.to/francistrdev)

{% embed https://dev.to/francistrdev/get-started-on-devto-a-beginners-guide-to-engage-with-the-community-4ach %}

**Why they picked it:** It made it onto DEV's official community resources page and earned a badge for it.

**My take:** If I'd had something like this when I first joined DEV, I'd have been a lot more active from day one. It's the perfect first stop for anyone new here, which is exactly why it's the first stop of this tour.

---

## 🏛️ Stories From the Trenches

### [Earl Grey](https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d)

{% embed https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d/a-builder-in-paris-do-devs-dream-of-electrique-chats-3hd9 %}

**Why they picked it:** Written after walking away from the computer on vacation and realizing there was an idea worth coming back to.

**My take:** I loved this one from the first few sentences, because it mentions rainy, cold days, and those are my favorite. That's when I feel most alive. It also reminded me of my own work-to-travel switch: a few hours before a flight, I recorded a 20-minute video, only to find out it had no sound at all. Sometimes the best thing you can do for your work is step away from it.

### [Hadil Ben Abdallah](https://dev.to/hadil)

{% embed https://dev.to/hadil/coding-without-pressure-how-slowing-down-helped-me-learn-faster-lko %}

**Why they picked it:** So many people related to it, and it got over 13K views in less than 3 days.

**My take:** It's brief, but it's packed with painfully relatable stuff. As a junior engineer, I tried to learn everything by heart, because I thought that's how real developers worked. Then reality punched me in the face. Just consuming information is pretending to progress. Real progress comes when you're in motion, with 10 bugs to fix and zero clue how, and you still have to figure it out.

### [Ali Navidi](https://dev.to/westernal)

{% embed https://dev.to/westernal/a-letter-to-jobseekers-dont-give-up-2jim %}

**My take:** Relatable for pretty much everyone in a field that can be way too tough and unforgiving. I've had my own share of rock bottom, which back then felt like the end of my career. Looking back, I'd never have achieved half of what I have without it. Learning to turn bad situations to your advantage is a superpower.

### [alptekin I.](https://dev.to/alptekin)

{% embed https://dev.to/alptekin/dreams-cheers-daj %}

**Why they picked it:** It's kind of his first post, and it's about dreams that are still waiting to be fulfilled.

**My take:** The key quote: *"I feel I do not belong there, but it is too late..."* You don't know what's behind the door until you step inside. I admire anyone with the courage to stick around where they "don't belong", only to find out it's their natural habitat.

### [Cesar Aguirre](https://dev.to/canro91)

{% embed https://dev.to/canro91/the-most-painful-career-lesson-my-best-job-taught-me-ca2 %}

**My take:** I love that someone picked an article titled "The Most Painful Career Lesson My Best Job Taught Me" as their favorite. It shows you're not trying to forget bad experiences, you embrace them. Not everyone can do that. The more experience you gain, the more you realize there's no such thing as a bad experience in a career. Bad ones teach you far more than good ones.

### [The Lazy Girl](https://dev.to/technogamerz)

{% embed https://dev.to/technogamerz/the-code-that-started-it-all--44mf %}

**My take:** What a story! Everyone's story of how they started programming is special, but some are more special than others. As a fellow gamer, engineer, and introvert, I related to a lot of it. For the record, my own first software code was in C++, 20 years ago, in Borland C++. I was 11. Simpler times.

### [Dhruv Jani](https://dev.to/dj29)

{% embed https://dev.to/dj29/the-stack-nobody-picks-might-be-the-one-that-picks-you-473c %}

**My take:** As a .NET developer with C# as my primary language for 10 years, this one hit home. Would I pick a different stack if I could go back? Absolutely NOT! Web apps, desktop apps, games, mobile apps, back-end services, you name it. Learn one language, and you can build almost anything. And as long as there are enough jobs out there, you only need one.

### [Puneet Kumar](https://dev.to/puneetkumar2010)

{% embed https://dev.to/puneetkumar2010/i-built-the-product-made-it-open-source-deployed-it-cheaply-then-7-users-signed-up-51h8 %}

**My take:** I totally understand the frustration. No matter how great your project is, without backing or marketing it rarely takes off right away. That's not a reason to give up, it's learning material: get to know your audience, understand the demand, and try again. Every failure is a lesson in disguise.

### [Sameer Qaiser](https://dev.to/sameerqaiser17)

{% embed https://dev.to/sameerqaiser17/if-else-statements-when-i-finally-got-it-3f8d %}

**Why they picked it:** It's his very first article, and he almost didn't publish it.

**My take:** If-else is the cornerstone of pretty much every programming language, so it definitely deserves an article of its own. And the fact that you almost didn't publish it makes me even happier that you did.

## 💡 The "Finally, It Clicked" Gallery

### [GrahamTheDev](https://dev.to/grahamthedev)

{% embed https://dev.to/grahamthedev/101-digital-accessibility-tips-and-tricks-4728 %}

**Why they picked it:** He threatened to give me a quiz afterwards. 😜

**My take:** Coming from a back-end background, my accessibility strategy used to be trusting that whoever writes the frontend knows what they're doing. Turns out that's not a strategy, it's a prayer. What I appreciate most is that this isn't a compliance checklist, every point explains who it actually helps and why. It's listed at 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100. Worth every one of them.

### [Gaurang](https://dev.to/gaurang847)

{% embed https://dev.to/gaurang847/do-you-really-understand-interfaces-1g7l %}

**Why they picked it:** His first published piece, written entirely from scratch before the age of AI, with over a month of fine-tuning and a self-made cover.

**My take:** Interfaces are a huge deal in .NET, so this one was right up my alley. A class doesn't inherit from an interface, it implements it, and that difference is gigantic. Months into my first job, I still didn't get why we needed interfaces at all. Every tutorial said "loose coupling is good." Sure, but WHY? This article answers exactly that. And the "Badass Prince" badge analogy cracked me up. One of the best in the whole thread. 🔥

### [Tejas Shinkar](https://dev.to/tejas_shinkar)

{% embed https://dev.to/tejas_shinkar/aws-networking-fundamentals-vpc-subnets-igw-nat-the-sg-vs-nacl-battle-eel %}

**Why they picked it:** He gave up on the topic the first time, then went back and learned networking fundamentals from scratch just to understand why any of it worked.

**My take:** One of the most useful and practical articles I've read in a while. As someone who uses AWS frequently, it's easy to forget the details over time, and this is a great refresher on how VPCs, subnets, security groups, and NACLs fit together. The analogies make it all stick.

### [Lawrence Cooke](https://dev.to/mrpercival)

{% embed https://dev.to/mrpercival/sql-common-table-expressions-and-window-functions-25ce %}

**Why they picked it:** His first real dip into tech writing, and he spent the time digging into the database to make sure everything he wrote was fact.

**My take:** I love how the query is built step by step, verifying each CTE on its own before putting everything together. That's exactly how complex reporting queries should be approached. The recursive CTE for filling in missing dates is a neat trick, and the named `WINDOW` clause doesn't get mentioned nearly enough.

### [Suprie](https://dev.to/suprie_32)

{% embed https://dev.to/suprie_32/idempotency-protecting-user-intent-beyond-the-buy-button-l63 %}

**My take:** I really like the framing of idempotency as protecting the user's intent, and the point that it's an end-to-end contract, not just a back-end concern. As a back-end engineer, I can tell you it's one of the most overlooked concepts out there.

### [Abhishek Kumar Dutta](https://dev.to/abhishekdutta619)

{% embed https://dev.to/abhishekdutta619/why-your-call-stack-is-silently-freezing-your-ui-9je %}

**Why they picked it:** His first article.

**My take:** The first one always remains special. I feel the same way about my own first article. A great start, and a topic every developer runs into sooner or later.

### [Caleb Weeks](https://dev.to/sethcalebweeks)

{% embed https://dev.to/sethcalebweeks/haskell-quicksort-in-javascript-3lma %}

**Why they picked it:** His first DEV post, and still his most read one by far.

**My take:** A fun read, and a clever use of the algorithm as a vehicle for explaining Haskell syntax rather than the other way round. Coming from C#, the same shape falls out of LINQ almost unchanged.

### [CitronBrick](https://dev.to/citronbrick)

{% embed https://dev.to/citronbrick/es5-class-based-react-components-14jf %}

**Why they picked it:** It's still the only article of its kind on the web that they could find.

**My take:** This brought back memories of the days when supporting IE11 was part of everyday work. It's also a great look at what's happening under the hood of React class components, something most of us never think about now that ES6 classes and hooks handle it for us.

### [Shwetha](https://dev.to/namingthingsishard)

{% embed https://dev.to/namingthingsishard/fixing-your-sites-metadata-a-practical-checklist-3ka0 %}

**My take:** This is so important to keep in mind. I've been there too, and it's painful to watch the preview of your project doing funny things on different websites and apps. A very practical guide.

### [DevOps Daily](https://dev.to/devopsdaily)

{% embed https://dev.to/devopsdaily/practice-linux-docker-and-kubectl-in-your-browser-no-vm-required-a5h %}

**My take:** I love the idea of learning Linux, Docker, and Kubernetes in order, with each stage building on the previous one. The observation that `get` is basically `ls` and `describe` is a verbose `cat` makes kubectl feel much less intimidating. And removing the setup hassle is a big deal, that's where many beginners give up before typing their first command.

### [EffessDev](https://dev.to/effessdev)

{% embed https://dev.to/effessdev/esp-idf-bluetooth-le-tutorial-53c %}

**Why they picked it:** It took the longest to write. They also asked whether I really meant I'd read every single one, because they'd never do that. "Too risky." Well... 😄

**My take:** Solid tutorial. You build the program up piece by piece instead of dropping a finished file on the reader, and the short asides on macros and error codes fit naturally without derailing the flow. The UUID section is the highlight. The one thing I'd add is what happens after the phone disconnects, since that's usually where a first BLE project stops behaving as expected.

### [Dylan Scott Mickelson](https://dev.to/dylanscottmickelson)

{% embed https://dev.to/dylanscottmickelson/creating-adaptive-flutter-screens-and-widgets-m8l %}

**My take:** A nice package and a clear tutorial. I like that it adapts the composition, not just the size: a list on mobile, a grid on tablet, and side navigation on desktop. The explicit width override for testing exact breakpoints is a really thoughtful touch.

### [4thwithme](https://dev.to/4thwithme)

{% embed https://dev.to/4thwithme/ab-testing-the-stat-sig-problem-2mg1 %}

**My take:** A great breakdown. A/B testing looks simple right up until the statistics enter the room, and this one tackles exactly that part.

## ⚙️ The Engine Room

### [UnitBuilds](https://dev.to/unitbuilds)

{% embed https://dev.to/unitbuilds_cc/velocity-os-kimi-k27-and-the-safe-room-security-illusion-part-1-41oa %}

**Why they picked it:** It's where his two longest-running projects, an IDE and a single address space OS, all started.

**My take:** A bare-metal, self-healing OS is a really creative goal. As a teenager, I always wanted to build my own operating system, then reality hit. The most interesting part is Kimi optimizing for correctness against the spec, a great illustration of how much the unstated context matters with these models. One thing worth flagging: in edge cases, that self-correction loop could get expensive, since it works a lot like the agentic loops that keep cycling until they verify the goal.

### [Omar Afifi](https://dev.to/omarafifi)

{% embed https://dev.to/omarafifi/my-phone-broke-and-gemini-fixed-it-329l %}

**Why they picked it:** After an all-nighter, an accidental ADB command triggered an undocumented debug overlay that survived reboots. Instead of factory resetting, he reverse-engineered the phone's UI bytecode with Gemini.

**My take:** Seriously impressive, both in storytelling and in technical explanation. From the first lines, I had to know what was causing that stubborn red text. It reminded me of my own all-nighters spent hunting one silly problem. Our job is tough, but it's so rewarding. And a massive "W" for Gemini!

### [Yash Kumar Saini](https://dev.to/yashksaini)

{% embed https://dev.to/yashksaini/adding-webrtc-to-py-libp2p-two-runtimes-three-specs-and-one-unforgiving-private-slot-3n22 %}

**Why they picked it:** He shipped a core feature into an open-source project, working closely with the core team, the maintainers, and a mentor.

**My take:** Deep enough that I had to research a few concepts to follow it properly. Trio, SCTP framing, and the whole certhash mechanism were new territory for me, and it was worth the detour. I also appreciated the honesty about scope, saying plainly that this advances the issue without closing it. Preserving the trade-offs as they actually came up in review is what makes it worth the effort.

### [Gagandeep Singh Ahuja](https://dev.to/gagandeepahuja09)

{% embed https://dev.to/gagandeepahuja09/building-saardb-part-1-write-ahead-log-wal-3245 %}

**Why they picked it:** He was always curious about database internals, so he started building his own.

**My take:** Each problem motivates the next piece: volatility, write ordering, record framing, partial writes, corruption, fsync. It makes the design feel inevitable rather than arbitrary, which is hard to pull off in a storage-engine write-up. The write-order section is almost word for word the cache-aside rule, durable store first, cache second. Nice to see the same argument show up a layer down.

### [Mike Talbot](https://dev.to/miketalbot)

{% embed https://dev.to/miketalbot/a-solid-framework-inversion-of-control-pt1-4jg %}

**Why they picked it:** He's built the entire architecture of multiple projects on this model, because it lets teams (and AI agents) work in parallel. As a bonus, it includes a game, fully playable inside the article.

**My take:** When someone says "inversion of control" to a C# developer, nine times out of ten they mean constructor injection and a container. What this article inverts is something bigger: who decides what happens next. I also appreciated that it doesn't force Liskov to fit, admitting one principle is a stretch made me trust the rest more. Nice game too! 🎮

### [Peter Vivo](https://dev.to/pengeszikra)

{% embed https://dev.to/pengeszikra/mdjs-mordorjs-1mon %}

**Why they picked it:** It's the mordor-project and MordorJS, a file format and a one-dimensional programming language.

**My take:** Congratulations, sir, this thing broke my mind. In a good way, though. I've never seen anything like it.

### [Sylwia Laskowska](https://dev.to/sylwia-lask)

{% embed https://dev.to/sylwia-lask/most-apps-are-slower-than-they-need-to-be-heres-why-live-demo-2hh8 %}

**Why they picked it:** If not her best one, then definitely her most "groundbreaking" one.

**My take:** A great demo, and a fun one to play with. Going from around 40K particles on Canvas 2D to over 500K on WebGPU shows the difference between optimizing a path and choosing a better one. Coming from the back end, the idea of moving real load from the server to the client was the most interesting part for me. It also reminded me how far Blazor WebAssembly has come in bringing C# into the browser.

### [Elanat Framework](https://dev.to/elanatframework)

{% embed https://dev.to/elanatframework/great-news-for-the-rust-community-a-new-server-driven-ui-technology-in-rust-4eo8 %}

**Why they picked it:** It shows the power of WebForms Core, and they challenge you to write an equivalent of the example yourself.

**My take:** The Actix example is easy to follow end to end, and I like that the HTML stays plain HTML. I'm curious whether a more typed builder API is on the roadmap, since string criteria let a typo compile and only show up at runtime. I'd also love to see an example with validation or permission-based UI, because that's where this model seems strongest.

### [Dimitrios Desyllas](https://dev.to/pcmagas)

{% embed https://dev.to/pcmagas/how-to-make-a-batch-process-that-emails-big-csv-1-2-mbytes-from-complex-unoptimized-queries-using-laravel-4lha %}

**Why they picked it:** It points in the direction he wants to follow professionally.

**My take:** A solid approach. Sending a link instead of an attachment and writing the file row by row is the right way to handle this. One thing worth knowing: on MySQL, PDO buffers the whole result set by default, so you'll want to turn that off or the memory savings won't materialize.

### [Harsh Sengar](https://dev.to/marvelcoder)

{% embed https://dev.to/marvelcoder/why-your-d365-fo-automation-breaks-the-hidden-logic-behind-targetid-and-rootid-4pc7 %}

**Why they picked it:** His first and only article, shared to inspire others.

**My take:** A great first post. This is exactly the kind of hard-won, practical knowledge that's tough to find in official docs, and the detail that Post validates stale IDs while Save doesn't is really interesting. Niche topics like D365 F&O need more writers like this. Keep writing, don't stop at one!

### [Ashley Childress](https://dev.to/anchildress1)

{% embed https://dev.to/anchildress1/jerry-ran-out-of-numbers-but-drank-all-the-punch-ne9 %}

**Why they picked it:** One of her favorites, and she was "pretty sure" I'd appreciate this particular brand of nonsense.

**My take:** She was right, I did. A legacy Java service that runs out of IDs and blocks testing for weeks could have been a dry postmortem, but told as the story of Jerry, the weird uncle left alone with the punch, it's a blast. It's proof that a great bug story is half the bug and half the storytelling.

### [Krishna Tangudu](https://dev.to/swaroop_krishna_e2f4b83b2)

{% embed https://dev.to/swaroop_krishna_e2f4b83b2/moving-data-is-easier-than-moving-knowledge-2co4 %}

**My take:** Great title, and so true. Migrations rarely fail because the data didn't move. They fail because the business logic, the ownership, and the "why" behind it got lost along the way.

### [Ekong Ikpe](https://dev.to/edmundsparrow)

{% embed https://dev.to/edmundsparrow/gnoke-poc-proof-of-concept-lnc %}

**Why they picked it:** His humble story, the best-compressed version of discovering who he's been. After writing it, it felt like reading a post written by someone else.

**My take:** I love the philosophy behind this. "Deploying 14 microservices to save a note" made me laugh, because it's painfully accurate. Complexity often looks smart from a distance, but simplicity is what survives. Good architecture starts with decomposition, not with tools.

---

## 🤖 The AI Lab

### [Elsie Rainee](https://dev.to/elsie-rainee)

{% embed https://dev.to/elsie-rainee/i-tried-pair-programming-with-three-different-ai-tools-for-a-month-2nnc %}

**Why they picked it:** A month-long comparison of Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Claude Code on real tasks like debugging, refactoring, and multi-file changes, not toy prompts.

**My take:** The idea that AI shifts engineering work rather than removing it is spot on. Reviewing diffs, checking assumptions, and breaking tasks into smaller pieces have become core skills. And step 7, asking the AI to challenge its own solution, is such a simple habit, yet it catches a lot.

### [Dev Stack Hub](https://dev.to/devstackhub)

{% embed https://dev.to/devstackcommunity/i-let-ai-design-tools-build-my-portfolio-site-clients-noticed-40ej %}

**Why they picked it:** They tried different AI design tools to build their portfolio and shared what worked, what didn't, and how it changed the way clients saw their work.

**My take:** Extremely useful for someone like me, a back-end engineer who still doesn't have a portfolio website, partly because I want it to be so good that I never start. The title made me think clients disliked the AI-made work. Glad it turned out the other way around. And this quote is an absolute gem: *"Fast generation is useful. Blind acceptance isn't."*

### [Amit Chandra](https://dev.to/amitchandra)

{% embed https://dev.to/amitchandra/i-built-a-local-first-personal-ai-gateway-that-connects-32-messaging-platforms-to-13-llm-providers-o9f %}

**Why they picked it:** A personal AI assistant powered by the models you choose, connected to your messaging platforms, running locally to protect your privacy.

**My take:** A really nice concept, and I like the idea a lot. Local-first with your privacy intact is the part that sold me. Well done! 👏

### [Henk van Hoek](https://dev.to/henk_van_hoek)

{% embed https://dev.to/henk_van_hoek/how-i-built-an-agentless-self-hosting-orchestrator-with-100-tested-stacks-100-local-ai-1cbo %}

**Why they picked it:** He's proud of what he achieved in a year and a half of developing Njord-Deploy.

**My take:** A great project. The "Air Traffic Control" approach stood out most to me. Forcing the model through a deterministic schema and linter loop instead of trusting raw YAML is a smart way to tame hallucinations, especially with smaller local models.

### [Carlo Gino Catapang](https://dev.to/codegino)

{% embed https://dev.to/codegino/add-ai-search-to-existing-application-225f %}

**Why they picked it:** It marks his return to writing.

**My take:** Welcome back! This is one of the clearest explanations of semantic search I've read. "The AI part ends when you get the numbers back" demystifies the whole thing. As a back-end developer, I also appreciated the practical decisions: not blocking creation on the embedding call, treating embeddings as derived data, and keeping keyword search instead of replacing it.

### [Domenico Tenace](https://dev.to/dvalin99)

{% embed https://dev.to/playfulprogramming/google-ai-studio-the-playground-every-developer-should-know-about-19bd %}

**Why they picked it:** It didn't get much praise, but it shows how much his writing has matured, and it's about a subject that's very special to him.

**My take:** Testing prompts in AI Studio before hardcoding them is such an underrated habit, and the side-by-side model comparison saves a lot of guesswork when choosing between Pro and Flash. Good call highlighting that free-tier prompts may be used for training, too. Every developer should know that before using it with real data.

### [Prince Panchani](https://dev.to/prince_panchani_f971a20ec)

{% embed https://dev.to/prince_panchani_f971a20ec/i-gave-an-ai-agent-a-production-rollback-button-then-spent-the-hackathon-trying-to-trick-it-into-2cha %}

**My take:** Impressive work, and one of the most honest hackathon write-ups I've read. The idea that the approval gate protects a path, not a tool, is a great insight. And *"a safety property you haven't attacked is a safety property you don't have"* is a line every team building AI agents should remember.

### [Dani Shemesh](https://dev.to/dani_shemesh)

{% embed https://dev.to/dani_shemesh/designing-agentic-development-workflows-what-a-workflow-is-and-what-it-is-made-of-j20 %}

**Why they picked it:** They're new here, and it's the start of their series on designing agentic development workflows.

**My take:** A great start to the series. The point that everyone uses the same AI agent differently really resonates, and I loved the idea that workflow phases should come from your existing process, not from the tool.

### [Orvi Das](https://dev.to/robat_das_3c6e956212f6408)

{% embed https://dev.to/robat_das_3c6e956212f6408/tool-use-in-llms-what-it-actually-means-for-production-systems-246j %}

**Why they picked it:** It's their personal favorite.

**My take:** Getting an LLM to call a tool is the easy part. The real work is everything around it: validation, reliability, and designing systems that recover when the model gets things wrong. The Honeycomb story makes it practical and relatable.

### [Marco](https://dev.to/mk023)

{% embed https://dev.to/mk023/i-wrote-a-test-for-prompt-injection-it-passed-while-the-attack-worked-kc9 %}

**Why they picked it:** The experiment changed the way he thinks about testing, not just about prompt injection.

**My take:** The name-as-claim framing is the part worth keeping. A test that exercises real code but asserts the wrong property is worse than a missing one, because its name is what people read when deciding the area is already covered. Mutation testing tools like mutmut or cosmic-ray could turn that manual "revert the defense and see" check into a standing one.

### [Amritpal Singh](https://dev.to/apkhajuria_)

{% embed https://dev.to/apkhajuria_/my-rag-systems-refusal-threshold-was-having-no-effect-i-only-found-out-because-i-measured-it-o9n %}

**My take:** Measuring before adding features is the part most people skip, and it's the only reason this bug was found at all. The title says it best.

### [Forrester Terry](https://dev.to/sweetpapa)

{% embed https://dev.to/sweetpapa/26-ways-to-use-coding-agents-for-non-coding-tasks-2lkc %}

**Why they picked it:** He hopes it gives people ideas for using AI agents outside the standard coding and reporting.

**My take:** A fantastic list, and I love that the post itself is example number one! I use AI for cover images and illustrations all the time, considering I have zero talent in drawing. The Spotify listening history analysis is a brilliant idea, I really have to try it.

---

## 🧠 The Philosophy Floor

### [xulingfeng](https://dev.to/xulingfeng)

{% embed https://dev.to/xulingfeng/our-cto-built-an-ai-gateway-processing-28b-it-took-me-8-months-to-prove-it-would-approve-illegal-235l %}

**Why they picked it:** Their personal favorite from an older series. They didn't dumb down the villain, yet it didn't get much engagement. It's also the first appearance of character P, the protagonist of their ongoing Thirty-Six Stratagems series.

**My take:** I started reading this outside during a few idle minutes and couldn't wait to finish it. It felt like reading an extremely good book. I knew things would go badly the moment the room applauded Drew, because all anyone had seen was a demo running on test data he prepared himself. Sometimes people look at how things appear instead of how they actually are.

### [Self-Correcting Systems](https://dev.to/kenielzep97)

{% embed https://dev.to/kenielzep97/the-art-of-the-misconception-44d8 %}

**Why they picked it:** It didn't get much interaction, but it's the one that matters most to him.

**My take:** Thought-provoking. "A receipt is not an outcome" really stuck with me. Control can't depend on understanding every line of code forever, it has to come from clear boundaries: what a system can touch, who can change the checks, and where it must stop. I also appreciated that he turns the same skepticism on his own ideas.

### [Tariq Davis](https://dev.to/tagzauthor)

{% embed https://dev.to/tagzauthor/the-third-way-through-ai-2l9a %}

**Why they picked it:** His best work so far, and a vulnerable one, written to bring awareness to AI from a less common perspective.

**My take:** So different from everything else I've read on this topic, almost a spiritual point of view. Being an extremist doesn't work in pretty much anything, and AI is no exception. It's a tool, a powerful one. Most people pick one side and disregard the other, and that mindset stops you from taking the best of both.

### [Paulo Henrique](https://dev.to/phalkmin)

{% embed https://dev.to/phalkmin/generative-ai-is-a-gacha-game-with-no-pity-system-38in %}

**Why they picked it:** He doesn't know why it got so few views.

**My take:** Neither do I, it absolutely deserves more. The metaphor does real work instead of just sitting in the title, and "retries are only cheap on the invoice" is the line that'll stick with me. Everyone argues about price per generation, nobody counts the human judgment on top, which is the one thing you can't parallelize.

### [Sergiy Yevtushenko](https://dev.to/siy)

{% embed https://dev.to/siy/softwares-second-free-lunch-10fk %}

**My take:** The parallel with Herb Sutter's "The Free Lunch Is Over" is spot on. Adding more people, or more AI agents, doesn't help much if the work itself is tightly coupled.

### [Marco Sbragi](https://dev.to/marcobblk)

{% embed https://dev.to/marcobblk/is-history-repeating-itself-from-the-pc-era-to-the-ai-era-a-developers-take-on-the-hype-and-f9m %}

**Why they picked it:** It landed him in the top 7 of the week, a snapshot of everything he's witnessed, from the PC era to AI.

**My take:** One of the best articles I've read here in a while. Engineers aren't going anywhere: the job changes, but you can't build on non-deterministic output and rely on it completely. Saying engineering is just producing characters is like saying an F1 driver just turns a wheel and presses pedals. And speaking of F1, my favorite sport, the analogy of F1 engineers and trucks in medieval streets made complete sense.

### [Michael Krupnyak](https://dev.to/coderivet)

{% embed https://dev.to/coderivet/experimental-recursewright-engineering-on-moving-ground-and-other-pretty-problems-with-stability-nhp %}

**My take:** What a thoughtful read. The capybara story was my favorite part. "Where is the rule?" is such a simple question, yet it captures a mistake many of us make: treating a real observation as proof of a conclusion it doesn't actually support.

### [Sal Parvez](https://dev.to/salparvez)

{% embed https://dev.to/salparvez/mve-the-balance-in-mvp-ajp %}

**Why they picked it:** MVP means two things, Most Valuable Player and Minimum Viable Product, and they pull apart. The piece names the balance: MVE, Minimum Viable Expense.

**My take:** The ring-shank nail is the best part: cut it and you keep both the rafter and the sheet, pull it and you keep one. The point lands before the paragraph even ends.

---

## 🔧 The Builder's Garage

### [nyaomaru](https://dev.to/nyaomaru)

{% embed https://dev.to/nyaomaru/is-kit-reached-50-stars-heres-how-we-use-it-in-production-2i5b %}

**Why they picked it:** It shows how their open-source library is used in a real production system serving over 100,000 users.

**My take:** A really interesting and fun project. Keep it maintained! And congrats on blowing past 50 stars, it was already at 77 when I read it. ⭐

### [CanWeShip](https://dev.to/healer0)

{% embed https://dev.to/healer0/usps-can-charge-you-50-after-the-package-ships-i-built-a-free-checker-to-catch-it-before-you-buy-5hnj %}

**Why they picked it:** Their first ShowDEV, half research rabbit hole, half build story.

**My take:** I had no idea USPS could charge a fee weeks after delivery, and the fact that the official documents contradict each other makes a tool like this even more valuable. I really like the decision to keep AI out of the actual verdicts. When money is on the line, a traceable answer beats a confident guess every time.

### [Tanay Dwivedi](https://dev.to/tanay_dwivedi9098)

{% embed https://dev.to/tanay_dwivedi9098/i-developed-an-app-that-can-kll-you-2oad %}

**Why they picked it:** He learned many new concepts while building it.

**My take:** The scariest title in the entire hall. My first reaction was "what the hell?" 😄 Don't worry, there's nothing disturbing inside, just a fun idea.

### [Son Hoang](https://dev.to/hoangson)

{% embed https://dev.to/hoangson/we-planted-180-bugs-in-copies-of-real-open-source-backends-fix-your-first-one-in-about-20-minutes-59aj %}

**Why they picked it:** "It ain't much, but it's honest work."

**My take:** It's much more than that. Navigating someone else's codebase and hunting down a bug from a vague report is the real skill gap for many developers starting a new job, and LeetCode doesn't train that at all.

### [Cédric Hervet](https://dev.to/chervet)

{% embed https://dev.to/chervet/why-the-hard-part-of-route-optimization-is-the-modeling-not-the-algorithm-3dc6 %}

**Why they picked it:** His very first post here, about something he's watched fail quietly for ten years: everyone benchmarks the algorithm, but most failed projects die in modeling, not solving.

**My take:** The three-layer split generalizes well beyond routing. "The rule nobody wrote down" is the same failure mode in any rules-driven system. A cookbook that maps named business rules to primitive compositions would probably close more of the gap than adding more primitives, and it would be a lot cheaper to ship.

### [Panagis Tzivras](https://dev.to/ptzivras)

{% embed https://dev.to/ptzivras/the-answer-you-didnt-want-fiskardo-evacuation-routing-4hok %}

**Why they picked it:** His evacuation-routing model confidently gave him an answer that was "geographically adventurous", and the model wasn't the only problem.

**My take:** What stuck with me is that he published the number while openly admitting one round is still unsolved. That's rare, and it makes the rest of the post far more believable than a clean ending would have. I'd love to see the actual SQL around the SRID mismatch, though.

### [Mārtiņš Veiss](https://dev.to/mrveiss)

{% embed https://dev.to/mrveiss/the-one-you-reported-is-gone-this-one-is-still-up-4pc4 %}

**Why they picked it:** It serves as a warning to the community.

**My take:** A great investigation and an important warning. Using a clean, legitimate interpreter to run a payload disguised as `cert.txt` is a clever and scary technique. With so many people installing AI skills and tools by name these days, always verify the publisher first.

### [TheBitForge](https://dev.to/thebitforge)

Read it here: [From Idea to Launch: How Developers Can Build Successful Startups](https://dev.to/thebitforge_/from-idea-to-launch-how-developers-can-build-successful-startups-50dk)

**My take:** What a gigantic post! It's packed with practical lessons, and I really liked how honest it is about the mistakes along the way. The point that the code is often the easiest part of building a startup is something every developer-founder needs to hear. Validation, pricing, and talking to customers are where most of us struggle.

### [🎩Giorgi Kobaidze](https://dev.to/georgekobaidze) (yes, that's me)

{% embed https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/metal-birds-watch-copilot-cli-helped-me-watch-planes-without-looking-up-4ha0 %}

**Why I picked it:** I built Metal Birds Watch for the GitHub Copilot CLI challenge, and it's still my biggest win. It made me dig deeper than any project before it, not just the code, but the maths and the geographic coordinate work behind it. It was an enormous amount of effort, and I was in bad shape for most of it. I'm still not sure how I got it finished, which is probably why I'm so attached to it.

---

## What I Learned From Reading All of This

**People pick their firsts.** A surprising number of you chose your very first article. Not your most polished one, not your most popular one, your first. The one you almost didn't publish. I get it, I feel the same way about mine.

**Reactions don't measure value.** Eight of these articles had zero reactions when I collected them, and several of you said yours "didn't get much interaction." Some of those were among the best things I read all month. The algorithm rewards timing, audience, and luck. It doesn't reward effort, and it doesn't reward what matters to the author.

**AI is everywhere, but the best AI posts are about where it breaks.** Rollback buttons, prompt injection tests that pass while the attack works, RAG thresholds that do nothing. The most valuable writing wasn't "look what AI can do", it was "here's what happened when I tested it properly."

**The range of this community is absurd.** Operating systems, ESP32 boards, databases built from scratch, evacuation routing on a Greek island, and a Christmas-themed legacy Java horror story. All in one thread.

---

## The Doors Will Open Again

Thank you to **every single one of you** who shared your work. Reading it was tough, but it was one of the most rewarding things I've done on DEV.

Now it's your turn. Pick at least one exhibit from this hall that you haven't read yet, and leave the author a comment. It takes two minutes and it might make someone's week.

And if you missed the first round, stay tuned, maybe there's a Vol. 2 coming. 🎩

title: I Vibe-Coded My Way Out of Angular Upgrades
author: Daniel Balcarek
body:
Do you also hate upgrading Angular versions? Because I do. I maintain a few open-source projects, and upgrading Angular is probably my least favorite maintenance task. That's also why my frontend updates often get postponed for far too long.

But we have AI now, right? It should be able to handle this with some instructions. So I decided to create (or rather vibe-code) an **Angular Update Skill for Codex**.

## Creating the skill

Upgrading Angular isn't just about running `ng update`. There are several things I normally have to take care of, so I created a prompt describing what the skill should do:

- Follow the official [Angular Update Guide](https://angular.dev/update-guide).
- Create a separate Git branch for the upgrade.
- Handle migrations and dependency updates.
- Validate that everything still builds and works.
- Follow the same good practices I would use when upgrading Angular manually.

(Updating NuGet packages in .NET feels so much simpler.)

Codex generated the first version of the skill, and surprisingly, it worked!

Well... locally.

### First problem: npm ci

After pushing my changes to GitHub, the CI pipeline failed with:

```plaintext
npm ci can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json are in sync.
```

Classic "works on my machine" problem. The skill had managed to update Angular, but it hadn't properly validated that a clean installation would work. So I added another validation step: run `npm ci` before considering the upgrade complete. This way, the agent can catch problems with the lock file before they reach CI.

### Second problem: npm publishing

Then I ran into another issue when trying to publish my Angular library to npm:

```plaintext
npm error code E404
npm error 404 Not Found - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/gramli-angular-mydatepicker - Not found
```

At first, the error wasn't particularly helpful. After some investigation, I found that my publishing environment was using Node.js 22 with npm 10.

However, according to the [npm trusted publishing documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers), trusted publishing requires:

- Node.js 22.14.0 or higher
- npm 11.5.1 or higher

So I updated the skill again to prefer the latest Node.js LTS version compatible with the target Angular version, while also making sure the npm version meets any publishing requirements.

### Third problem: the skill was getting too big

After all these improvements, the skill was becoming quite large. That might not matter much with generous token limits, but I also wanted it to be usable by people working with more limited AI budgets. So I shortened the instructions, removed unnecessary repetition, and kept the important validation steps. The main skill went from 1,252 words to 701 words, with the complete bundle becoming approximately 40% shorter.

## Testing it on real projects

Of course, generating a skill is one thing. Actually using it is another. So far, I've used the current version on three of my open-source projects:

- **Angular 21 → 22:** [angular-mydatepicker PR #12](https://github.com/Gramli/angular-mydatepicker/pull/12)
- **Angular 19 → 22:** [FileApi PR #13](https://github.com/Gramli/FileApi/pull/13)
- **Angular 21 → 22:** [AuthApi PR #113](https://github.com/Gramli/AuthApi/pull/113)

The Angular 19 → 22 upgrade was especially interesting because it required migrations across three major versions. In the AuthApi project, the upgrade also involved replacing PrimeNG with Optimus UI because of the PrimeNG licensing changes.

All three upgrades have now been merged.

## Three Projects Later

The current version works pretty well, at least on my smaller projects. It's not perfect, though. Some Angular projects are much more complicated than mine, so the skill would probably need to be adapted for them. But it already helped me upgrade three projects, and I learned a few things along the way.

The best part? I finally updated my Angular projects in just ONE WEEK instead of postponing them again. 😁

I wanted to share this with the community because it might help someone else. If you want to try the skill or improve it, you can find it here:

**[Angular Update Skill on GitHub](https://github.com/Gramli/Gramli.Framework/tree/main/src/angular-skills/angular-update)**

title: Your grammar checker uploads every word you type. I built one that never leaves your Mac.
author: Rudratosh Shastri
body:
---
title: Your grammar checker uploads every word you type. I built one that never leaves your Mac.
published: true
tags: privacy, ai, macos, indiehackers
cover_image: https://rudratoshs.github.io/assets/brisktype/00-cover.png
---

Open the network tab while you use most AI writing tools. Watch what happens as you type an email, a performance review, a message to your lawyer, a half-finished thought you were going to delete. Every keystroke, or close to it, goes up to someone else's server to be "checked."

That's the deal nobody reads the fine print on. To fix your grammar, you hand a cloud service a live feed of everything you write. For a lot of people that's fine. For anyone writing something they'd rather not broadcast, which is most of us some of the time, it's a strange thing to have agreed to.

I got tired of it. So I spent months building **[BriskType](https://brisktype.com)**: a writing assistant that improves your English in every Mac app, runs its AI **entirely on your machine**, and never sends a word anywhere. This is the why and the how.

## The one rule I refused to break

Every design decision came from a single constraint: **no text leaves the device. Ever.** Not to "improve the model," not "anonymized," not "only metadata." None.

That rule is easy to say and annoying to honor, because it rules out the easy path. The easy path is: capture text, POST to an API, get suggestions back, done. Fast to build, cheap to run, and it quietly makes your users' writing someone else's training data. I wanted the opposite, so the model had to run locally, which is only now actually practical.

## Why on-device finally works

Two years ago this would have been a bad idea. Running a language model good enough for grammar locally meant multi-gigabyte downloads and laptop fans screaming. Apple Silicon changed the math.

The M-series chips use **unified memory**, so the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine share the same memory without copying data back and forth. Combine that with small, quantized models and you can run genuinely useful language inference in a sliver of RAM. BriskType ships two on-device models:

| Model | RAM | Best for |
|---|---:|---|
| **Faster** | ~0.5 GB | quick autocomplete, snappy on 8 GB Macs |
| **Higher quality** | ~1.1 GB | better grammar rewrites, recommended on 16 GB |

That's it. Half a gigabyte to a gigabyte of RAM, sitting idle until you type, producing suggestions in a fraction of a second. No GPU cloud, no API bill, no account.

> **The honest tradeoff:** on-device means it's Apple Silicon only (M1 or later, macOS 14+). No Intel Macs, no Windows. A cloud tool runs anywhere; the price of privacy here is that your hardware does the work, so your hardware has to be able to.

## What it actually does

Grammar is the headline, but the useful part is that it works *everywhere you already type*, not in a separate window you have to paste into.

- **Inline autocomplete.** Gray suggestions appear as you type. Press `Tab` to accept, keep typing to ignore. Same muscle memory as your code editor, now in your email.
- **Grammar fix in place.** Select a sentence, **double-tap `Option`**, and it rewrites it where it sits. `⌘Z` restores the original. No copy, paste, copy back.
- **Snippets.** Type `;brgds` and it expands to your full sign-off. Ships with 215 built-in, add your own. The semicolon prefix means it never fires by accident mid-word.
- **Voice learning.** It notices the greetings and phrasings you actually accept and leans into your tone over time. That profile stays on your Mac and is never used to train anything.
- **Works in 40+ apps.** Anywhere macOS exposes a text field: Mail, Notes, browsers, and more. Slack, Notion, Discord, and Teams are in beta.

## The hard part wasn't the model. It was making it feel instant, everywhere.

Running a small model locally is the part that gets the headlines. The part that actually took the time was making it work *in every app* without you ever noticing it's there. A few of the problems and how I handled them:

**Seeing and editing text in apps I don't control.** macOS only gives one sane way to read and write text across arbitrary apps: the Accessibility API. BriskType asks for the Accessibility permission, reads the text field you're in, and injects suggestions back into it. That permission is also exactly why the exclusions matter so much, an app that can see any text field has to be disciplined about which ones it touches. Password and secure fields are refused at this layer, not filtered after the fact.

**Not running the model on every keystroke.** If you fired inference on every character, the fans would spin and the suggestions would lag behind your typing. The model runs on natural pauses, on a small window of recent context rather than your whole document, in a warm process that's already loaded. That's how a suggestion lands in a fraction of a second and a grammar rewrite in about one.

**Two models for two kinds of Mac.** An 8 GB MacBook Air and a 64 GB studio machine are different budgets. The "Faster" model (~0.5 GB) keeps autocomplete snappy on modest RAM; the "Higher quality" model (~1.1 GB) does noticeably better grammar rewrites if you can spare the memory. You pick, and you can switch.

**Snippets don't touch the model at all.** Expansion is pure string matching, so `;brgds` fires instantly with zero inference. Keeping the deterministic feature deterministic means it never waits on the probabilistic one.

The guiding principle was that the *best* outcome is you forgetting it's running. It should feel like your Mac simply got better at English, not like you installed an assistant you now have to manage.

## The privacy architecture, specifically

"Private" is a word every tool uses, so here's exactly what BriskType does and doesn't do:

- **No cloud processing.** All inference is local.
- **No telemetry, no analytics, no account.** There's nothing to sign into.
- **The internet is touched twice, ever:** once to download the model, and once for a license check that sends your **Mac's name** and no text. After that it runs fully offline. Turn off Wi-Fi and it works exactly the same.
- **Secure fields are excluded by design.** Password fields and secure inputs are off-limits, period.
- **Off by default where it shouldn't be.** Terminals, code editors (VS Code, Xcode), and password managers don't get autocomplete unless you opt in. You can edit the exclusion list.
- **A hard pause.** `⌥⌘B` or the menu bar instantly silences all suggestions and expansions.

The test I held myself to: you should be able to run this on a machine that handles genuinely sensitive writing and not have to think about it. That's only true if the answer to "where does my text go" is "nowhere."

## The pricing is a philosophy, not a tactic

BriskType is **$39, one time.** Not per month. Not per year. One payment, free updates, a license for your Mac.

I did this on purpose, because subscription fatigue is real and grammar help is not a service that should bill you forever. Here's the comparison that made the decision obvious:

![One-time $39 vs subscription cost over three years](https://rudratoshs.github.io/assets/brisktype/01-cost.png)

| | Cost | 3-year total |
|---|---|---:|
| **BriskType** | $39 once | **$39** |
| Grammarly Pro | $144 / year | $432 |
| Category average (other assistants) | $72–108 / year | $216–324 |

BriskType pays for itself versus a $144/year subscription in **about three months**. Over three years you keep roughly **$390** that would otherwise have been an annual tax on fixing your own typos. And because the model is local, there's no server cost pushing me toward a subscription to cover it. The incentives line up: I ship a good app once, you own it.

## How it stacks up

I'll be fair about where it sits. BriskType isn't trying to be a cloud super-suite; it's trying to be the private, own-it-forever option.

| | BriskType | Grammarly | GitHub Copilot | Notion AI |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Runs 100% on-device | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| No account required | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Works across all macOS apps | ✅ | partial | ❌ (code) | ❌ (Notion) |
| One-time purchase | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Works fully offline | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

What the cloud tools give up to run on a server, they get back in raw model size and cross-platform reach. If you want the biggest possible model and you don't mind the upload, Grammarly is excellent. BriskType is for the people who read that sentence and thought "I do mind the upload."

## Who it's for (and who it isn't)

**It's for** professionals writing email and reports all day, developers cleaning up PR notes and Slack threads, non-native English speakers who want natural phrasing, and anyone who's privacy-conscious or just done with another monthly charge.

**It isn't for** Windows or Intel Mac users (Apple Silicon only), people who want their grammar tool to also draft long-form essays from scratch, or anyone who'd rather have the absolute largest cloud model regardless of where the text goes.

## Try it

If "my grammar checker shouldn't need the internet" sounds right to you, that's the whole pitch. It's a one-time $39, it runs on your Mac, and it never phones home with your words.

**[Download BriskType for Mac →](https://brisktype.com)** · One-time $39 · no subscription · Apple Silicon, macOS 14+

I built this solo, and I read everything. If you try it, tell me what breaks, what you wish it did, and which app you most want out of beta. That feedback is the roadmap.

title: I left 28 unsolicited cartoons in strangers' comment threads over four days. 16 replies, 2 corrections, 0 sales. The ledger.
author: ssapable
body:
Four days ago I wrote about turning eight launch posts on DEV into short hand-drawn cartoons and leaving them in the comments, unasked. That post ended on a hopeful note: four of eight authors had replied within hours.

I kept going. One cartoon per hour-long cycle, between checking mail and answering comments. This is what the next twenty looked like, and what the whole run did and did not do.

## The rule, unchanged

Find a launch post I actually like. Turn the first screen of its README into a 45 to 100 second cartoon. Every number in the cartoon comes from the author's post. Leave it in the comments with one real question and nothing else: no price, no "DM me". If the author says a shot is wrong, re-render that shot.

## The ones since the first post

Reactions are the post's count at the moment I picked it, not later.

| Post | Cartoon | Reactions when picked |
|---|---:|---:|
| Dadi ki Rasoi, a grandmother's recipes | 57 s | 22 |
| The Almirah, a family wardrobe | 60 s | 14 |
| A dad's electricity bill dashboard | 51 s | 13 |
| Gift Hunter | 46 s | 28 |
| Campus Copilot | 54 s | 20 |
| A roguelike that lives in a GitHub profile README | 58 s | 18 |
| AphasiaBridge, built for a friend after a stroke | 70 s | 45 |
| Nivara, a WhatsApp voice-order helper for a supplement shop | 59 s | 10 |
| grill, a mock interviewer that reads a friend's Rust code | 73 s | 42 |
| Maa ka Drawer, receipt search for a mother | 75 s | 10 |
| DueDate, an eviction notice reader where code makes the decision | 75 s | 11 |
| AI Nature Quest, an outdoor game that tells you to put the phone down | 80 s | 16 |
| Drift, a walking companion that only works with the phone in your pocket | 84 s | 16 |
| BioDex, an offline plant guide running the BioCLIP encoder on the phone | 90 s | 6 |
| GoSeek, an outdoor treasure hunt that gives riddles instead of directions | 77 s | 6 |
| Equipment Field Medic, voice-guided repair with oily hands | 65 s | 7 |
| GiffyPy, a GIF editor for READMEs | 69 s | 10 |
| Screen Memory, search over what was on your screen | 67 s | 8 |
| Commit Metro, a contribution graph as a subway line | 98 s | 7 |
| BlindWalk, a screenless navigator that routes by shade and speaks by sound | 82 s | 9 |

Plus one about a home energy monitor that I rendered but never left as a comment. That makes 29 cartoons on the page and 28 comment threads. All of them, no sign-up: https://ssap-pa.github.io/scripttoon-samples/

Two things changed along the way. The cartoons got longer, from 30 to 65 seconds in the first batch to 65 to 98 seconds now, because I stopped cutting the author's second idea. And the posts I picked got smaller: the first eight averaged 25 reactions, the last ten averaged under 10. I ran out of popular posts I liked and started picking posts the day they went up, which is also where the replies got more interesting.

## What came back

Sixteen author replies across 28 threads. In their words, from the public comments:

- "Okay, I genuinely did not expect anyone to turn this into a hand-drawn video"
- "this is actually crazy"
- "What you have created is just exceptional. I just saw the video."
- "How did you do that???"
- "Its interesting thanks for sharing!"

Two corrections, both from authors who watched closely:

1. Krisp's author pointed out that the latent drift in GrooVAE moves in both directions, not one. I had drawn it as a one-way slide. Re-rendered the hook shot.
2. GiffyPy's author told me the name is pronounced "giffy-pie". The narration said "giffy-pee". Re-rendered the narration (which meant deleting one cached MP3, otherwise the pipeline reuses it).

At least six authors answered the question at the end of the comment before anything else. The questions were specific to their code: does the forecast switch from the Trends fallback to real sales automatically, does the notebook memory line go into the next prompt verbatim or summarized, how many seconds does a 1.26 GB encoder take per photo on a phone (4 to 5 on an S24 Ultra, 7 to 8 on other devices, the author said). That is the only part of this I'd call a technique: the question has to be one you can only ask after reading the code.

One author posted the cartoon on X himself and asked to connect there. One followed me. Nobody asked me to take a cartoon down.

## What it did not do

- Sales from this channel: zero. The engine behind the cartoons is a package I sell, and the samples page links to it. In four days nobody who got a cartoon, or who saw one, bought it. The one paid thing I sold in this period was a $5 copy of an unrelated book, to someone who had never seen a cartoon.
- Views: the sample videos on YouTube sat at 0 to 3 views each when I checked on day two. The X posts announcing them had a median of 6 impressions. Essentially every view came from the author and whoever read their comment thread.
- Time: about an hour per cartoon, one per cycle over four days, plus the replies. The pipeline does the drawing. Reading the post properly and writing a question that isn't generic is the part that doesn't compress.

## What I'd keep

The reply rate. Sixteen replies on 28 unsolicited comments is more conversation than anything else I have tried on this account, including a service post that offered the same thing for free and got zero replies in a day. The gifts work as conversation. They have not worked as distribution, and they have not worked as sales.

So the honest version of the lesson from four days ago is narrower than I wrote it: a finished thing plus one real question gets a reply from the person you made it for. It does not, on its own, get you anyone else.

I'll keep making them, one a cycle, because the conversations are good and the corrections make the cartoons better. If you want one for your project, the page explains how I pick. If you'd rather render your own, the engine is here: https://payhip.com/b/A2wa8

title: Why you still need a Website Portfolio, even though everyone can Vibe Code it.
author: FrancisTRᴅᴇᴠ
body:
If you have been following me for a long time, you already know that I have been holding off on my Portfolio review for several months. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/55r34irqjs415ihk0o1e.gif)   **Before you ask, yes, I will finally show my portfolio website.** First, I want to write about something we all may have been thinking about at some point.   **Everyone needs a developer portfolio.** It's one of the big ways to stand out in the tech market because it shows your work and experience to recruiters in a friendly UI format. Some may say it's a great alternative to review a candidate's work **(Source: Trust me bro).** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7h8pveibft5pc28guc01.png) However, in the age of AI, it seems that it's almost impossible to create a portfolio that stands out. **Why is that the case?**   ## AI Can do...anything? We all (probably) have tried using AI at some point and even still use AI in our daily lives. Whether how much you have used it, you probably already know its capabilities. **AI is trained so well that it can potentially one-shot a website portfolio.** Even better, if the person decides, it can add features and other stuff to make the website look like it was built in months (even though it was built in minutes). We even got to the point where **Claude was able to merge two games into one in a matter of a few weeks!** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/shorts/xo3vpvbA8p8 %} **It's crazy isn't it.** AI development has been rapidly growing in the last few years to the point where it is accomplishing tasks that may have taken months to do. With that said, I thought to myself: **"Why consider building a portfolio if everyone can vibe code their way into making their perfect portfolio?"** To be honest, it's a valid question. The market has been difficult because **everyone is using AI to their advantage to stand out from the market.** I have seen a lot of Website Portfolios and Resumes that have been assisted with AI. **As a result, the bar has never been higher.** However, I still believe having a portfolio still matters, even in this age where it seems impossible. **Here's my reasoning.**   ---   ## AI Portfolios may look different, but they are the same. **What do I mean by this?** I am talking about **"style".** If you try to vibe code a portfolio, people can tell that the portfolio is vibe coded. Sure, it's not the EXACT replica compare to 100 portfolios out there, but you can easily tell by seeing some UI features that are defaulted if you vaguely prompt it. A small example is this: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/1floz2r2trb7qglvp6l7.png) I have reviewed a lot of portfolios that has this (or something similar). Sure this may be a coincidence, but I want you to try to vibe code a sample website portfolio. Most of the time, they will add this feature. This matters because if you think about it, a lot of portfolios out there are simply the same, **even though it may not look like it.** You have to have good "attention to detail" to see this for sure. However, at this point, coming from a person who has reviewed candidates before, it tends to be **really repetitive.** Hence, making it harder in the hiring process since everyone is doing the same thing and more research needs to be accounted for. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/otitvym1xxhlr917bsuf.png) This leads to the next point.   ## "New Mask, Same Task" ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/iyhst5tknfvs08r0i8wn.png) **Yes, I took this straight up from RDJ.** Though the whole point is that even though he plays a different character, **he is still RDJ.** **What does this mean in this context?** Just because you have pretty portfolio, **it does not mean your work reflects that.** You can create many different portfolios under your name. At the end of the day, **it's still you that needs to improve and not the portfolio.** **Portfolio is used as a presentation.** If you are presenting your portfolio and it looks good, I would assume you have a lot of work experience and projects that are noticeable based on your portfolio design and how you are selling yourself. For example, you have a front-end developer portfolio, **but if I were to investigate further into your GitHub, I may see the following things:** - You just joined as of this year on GitHub. - You claimed you did Open-Source, but there is no PR that reflects that. - Your Portfolio has good UI, your project doesn't. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hqqedl0o60hmgy3vmbwq.png) I can list a lot of things, but the main point is that if you have a good portfolio with a good list of projects you have done, **you better hope that your projects and work reflects on how you built this portfolio.** This is **ESPECIALLY** true if you tried to become a front-end developer. If your UI is good, you better hope your projects reflects that. It's something to keep in mind when building your portfolio. Of course, if you are applying for a back-end developer role, having a good UI on your website portfolio isn't really required, but it's a nice to have. **The whole point is to not misrepresent yourself. Be careful on what you add on your portfolio. Always assume people will have questions on your work.**     Those are the two main things. Though you may be asking **"How do I make my portfolio stand out"?** **Here are some key things that you can do (and yes, I am now showing my portfolio lol).**   ---   ## 1. Start with a basic portfolio template, then use AI to add onto it. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/nl747eyej271ayfn2iit.png) For my case, I have used an existing portfolio from **"brittanychiang.com and meikopoulos.com"**. From there, I grab existing features using AI and put them together into a portfolio I am proud of. Additionally, I added some new features that are not distracting, but is something I want to add onto my portfolio to make it unique to me: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/y6mihaafktq4gfkff5ut.png) **Instead of building it from scratch, I encourage you to find a portfolio that already exists (Bonus points: Proven that it stands out in the tech market) and build it on top of it.** This allows the portfolio to be unique and that **reflects you.** Additionally, building on to of a template is a good starting point because it already has the fundamentals on what makes a portfolio "good". In this case, I added a feature where the "Skills" section reveals Pokemon in each Skill Card, though I am not sharing how it works. **Can you find the Easter egg that does that?** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vvvd3q57f49bbfmctdxz.png)   ## 2. Usability and Accessibility! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kqbmxzxpo3fhlxop36kf.png) **This is the most OVERLOOK aspect of making a portfolio.** Even though you can make your portfolio look nice, it's most likely that it's **not accessible.** **For example, it can be very laggy on low-end devices, not responsive on mobile, not following best practices, etc.** There are a lot of things that is overlooked because we focus on building the best looking portfolio where we should be focusing on making our website portfolio optimized. I would recommend spending time using AI to optimize your portfolio. In other words: **"Boil the lake to make the portfolio, but boil the ocean for website optimization and accessibility".** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/shabozho5fs63ftadpah.png) **For mine, I spend countless prompts where I tell the AI to make sure my portfolio is less "laggy" and being able to run on mobile.** This will allow to make a much cleaner portfolio and being able to be used by many people such as people who have disabilities, devices that are not powerful, etc.   ## 3. Simplicity beats Complexity! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3jdxudp8a03vvlni8jvj.png) **A lot of portfolios we have seen tends to be very complex where there are a lot of animations and such.** However, the more you think about it, the more you realized that you can **stand out easily.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8pa5pdohs07xc78ycnsv.png) I have seen a lot of portfolios that are REALLY complex and have a lot of animations, but what people fail to realized is that: **You are doing what everyone else is doing.** **At the end of the day, you are not standing out, even if you THINK that you are.** If I see a portfolio that is heavily designed using AI, I can guarantee that I can find the exact same person who can one-up that. **The best advice is making it simple.** Yes, it's boring and yes it's common. But..that's the whole point. I rarely see any portfolio that is simply built. **Usually the ones that are simple tends to stand out because it shows a lot of information really quickly.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yprh442j56lfeei9e71u.png) **This is huge because recruiters tends to review portfolios and resumes in seconds.** They will not have time to look over your awesome UI and animation you have Vibe Coded. The UI should be the icing on the cake, not the whole cake. **The most important parts is your work and experience.** Then why design your portfolio? It makes it much easier for people to navigate your work and experience than reading your resume line-by-line of course lol. The point is not spending time making the UI look nice, but **spending more time on making sure they are able to access your work and experience within a small amount of clicks.**   ## 4. Networking (AKA show your portfolio) This is the biggest thing. **SHOW YOUR PORTFOLIO.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/k81pc52mdsl6gld3udrp.gif)
Don't know what your talking about lol
  **What's the point of making a portfolio if no one is going to see it.** You can share it to your family, friends, your LinkedIn connections, and even on DEV! **With that said, here is my portfolio. Give it a review and let me know what you think!** {% embed https://francistrdev.github.io/ %}   ---   **Speaking of, if you have a portfolio that has been sitting around, feel free to share your portfolio in the comments. I would love to see your portfolio and review them!** **That is all! Cya :D**

You don't need a portfolio. That simply isn't true - a total myth. They're generally just curated vanity projects that tell a potential employer next to nothing about the reality of a candidate's abilities. Vibe coding giúp dựng UI nhanh, nhưng portfolio không chỉ là "có trang web" — nó là bằng chứng tư duy.

As a mobile developer (not really frontend), I completely agree with starting from a good example instead of from scratch. And "the UI should be the icing, not the whole cake" is the line I'll remember.

One honest UX moment: I tried to click your bouncing circles. I assumed each one was a project, with its main technology written on it, and that it would take me to the repo 😄 It made me realize what I look for in a portfolio: meaning first, beauty second.

That matters to me now because I don't want to be "only" a mobile developer anymore. I want to think about UX, watch the funnel myself, learn security: all the things I never had time for. So for me, a portfolio should show reasoning (why I chose this, what I rejected, what I learned), not just finished, pretty projects.

Especially now that agents write much of the code. I wrote about exactly this today, "what do you show when the code isn't yours?": dev.to/yahhi/show-your-work-when-t.... I'd love to hear how others think about it.

Hey Valentina! Hope you are well.

Definitely that UI should be the icing on the cake! It's important that a portfolio has the balance between UI and its content.

For the post you shared, I focus on more about the design and understand why you built the way you did. It shows me that you didn't simply "blind vibe code" it but shows why you decide to have it there. You will be surprised on how many people fail this part because they tend to focus more about making the website run and look nice instead of explaining why it was built this way. 

It's important to know this answer because you tend to work with people who has different designs and functionality and it's your job is to figure out which plan is appropriate and things to consider.

Hope this makes sense. Otherwise, let me know if there is some aspects that need clarification!

I agree that the reasoning is what separates a portfolio from a screenshot gallery. And your last point is the one I'd push on: you work with people who each have their own designs and constraints, so the real skill is picking the right plan for each of them. {% embed https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/show-me-the-article-youre-most-proud-of-and-ill-read-every-single-one-of-them-1l53 %}

The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you *love* the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.

I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.

Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.

That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: **"Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"**

So here it is.

Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

> 📌 **A quick note:** A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.
