**Why they picked it:** He hopes it gives people ideas for using AI agents outside the standard coding and reporting.

**My take:** A fantastic list, and I love that the post itself is example number one! I use AI for cover images and illustrations all the time, considering I have zero talent in drawing. The Spotify listening history analysis is a brilliant idea, I really have to try it.

---

## 🧠 The Philosophy Floor

### [xulingfeng](https://dev.to/xulingfeng)

{% embed https://dev.to/xulingfeng/our-cto-built-an-ai-gateway-processing-28b-it-took-me-8-months-to-prove-it-would-approve-illegal-235l %}

**Why they picked it:** Their personal favorite from an older series. They didn't dumb down the villain, yet it didn't get much engagement. It's also the first appearance of character P, the protagonist of their ongoing Thirty-Six Stratagems series.

**My take:** I started reading this outside during a few idle minutes and couldn't wait to finish it. It felt like reading an extremely good book. I knew things would go badly the moment the room applauded Drew, because all anyone had seen was a demo running on test data he prepared himself. Sometimes people look at how things appear instead of how they actually are.

### [Self-Correcting Systems](https://dev.to/kenielzep97)

{% embed https://dev.to/kenielzep97/the-art-of-the-misconception-44d8 %}

**Why they picked it:** It didn't get much interaction, but it's the one that matters most to him.

**My take:** Thought-provoking. "A receipt is not an outcome" really stuck with me. Control can't depend on understanding every line of code forever, it has to come from clear boundaries: what a system can touch, who can change the checks, and where it must stop. I also appreciated that he turns the same skepticism on his own ideas.

### [Tariq Davis](https://dev.to/tagzauthor)

{% embed https://dev.to/tagzauthor/the-third-way-through-ai-2l9a %}

**Why they picked it:** His best work so far, and a vulnerable one, written to bring awareness to AI from a less common perspective.

**My take:** So different from everything else I've read on this topic, almost a spiritual point of view. Being an extremist doesn't work in pretty much anything, and AI is no exception. It's a tool, a powerful one. Most people pick one side and disregard the other, and that mindset stops you from taking the best of both.

### [Paulo Henrique](https://dev.to/phalkmin)

{% embed https://dev.to/phalkmin/generative-ai-is-a-gacha-game-with-no-pity-system-38in %}

**Why they picked it:** He doesn't know why it got so few views.

**My take:** Neither do I, it absolutely deserves more. The metaphor does real work instead of just sitting in the title, and "retries are only cheap on the invoice" is the line that'll stick with me. Everyone argues about price per generation, nobody counts the human judgment on top, which is the one thing you can't parallelize.

### [Sergiy Yevtushenko](https://dev.to/siy)

{% embed https://dev.to/siy/softwares-second-free-lunch-10fk %}

**My take:** The parallel with Herb Sutter's "The Free Lunch Is Over" is spot on. Adding more people, or more AI agents, doesn't help much if the work itself is tightly coupled.

### [Marco Sbragi](https://dev.to/marcobblk)

{% embed https://dev.to/marcobblk/is-history-repeating-itself-from-the-pc-era-to-the-ai-era-a-developers-take-on-the-hype-and-f9m %}

**Why they picked it:** It landed him in the top 7 of the week, a snapshot of everything he's witnessed, from the PC era to AI.

**My take:** One of the best articles I've read here in a while. Engineers aren't going anywhere: the job changes, but you can't build on non-deterministic output and rely on it completely. Saying engineering is just producing characters is like saying an F1 driver just turns a wheel and presses pedals. And speaking of F1, my favorite sport, the analogy of F1 engineers and trucks in medieval streets made complete sense.

### [Michael Krupnyak](https://dev.to/coderivet)

{% embed https://dev.to/coderivet/experimental-recursewright-engineering-on-moving-ground-and-other-pretty-problems-with-stability-nhp %}

**My take:** What a thoughtful read. The capybara story was my favorite part. "Where is the rule?" is such a simple question, yet it captures a mistake many of us make: treating a real observation as proof of a conclusion it doesn't actually support.

### [Sal Parvez](https://dev.to/salparvez)

{% embed https://dev.to/salparvez/mve-the-balance-in-mvp-ajp %}

**Why they picked it:** MVP means two things, Most Valuable Player and Minimum Viable Product, and they pull apart. The piece names the balance: MVE, Minimum Viable Expense.

**My take:** The ring-shank nail is the best part: cut it and you keep both the rafter and the sheet, pull it and you keep one. The point lands before the paragraph even ends.

---

## 🔧 The Builder's Garage

### [nyaomaru](https://dev.to/nyaomaru)

{% embed https://dev.to/nyaomaru/is-kit-reached-50-stars-heres-how-we-use-it-in-production-2i5b %}

**Why they picked it:** It shows how their open-source library is used in a real production system serving over 100,000 users.

**My take:** A really interesting and fun project. Keep it maintained! And congrats on blowing past 50 stars, it was already at 77 when I read it. ⭐

### [CanWeShip](https://dev.to/healer0)

{% embed https://dev.to/healer0/usps-can-charge-you-50-after-the-package-ships-i-built-a-free-checker-to-catch-it-before-you-buy-5hnj %}

**Why they picked it:** Their first ShowDEV, half research rabbit hole, half build story.

**My take:** I had no idea USPS could charge a fee weeks after delivery, and the fact that the official documents contradict each other makes a tool like this even more valuable. I really like the decision to keep AI out of the actual verdicts. When money is on the line, a traceable answer beats a confident guess every time.

### [Tanay Dwivedi](https://dev.to/tanay_dwivedi9098)

{% embed https://dev.to/tanay_dwivedi9098/i-developed-an-app-that-can-kll-you-2oad %}

**Why they picked it:** He learned many new concepts while building it.

**My take:** The scariest title in the entire hall. My first reaction was "what the hell?" 😄 Don't worry, there's nothing disturbing inside, just a fun idea.

### [Son Hoang](https://dev.to/hoangson)

{% embed https://dev.to/hoangson/we-planted-180-bugs-in-copies-of-real-open-source-backends-fix-your-first-one-in-about-20-minutes-59aj %}

**Why they picked it:** "It ain't much, but it's honest work."

**My take:** It's much more than that. Navigating someone else's codebase and hunting down a bug from a vague report is the real skill gap for many developers starting a new job, and LeetCode doesn't train that at all.

### [Cédric Hervet](https://dev.to/chervet)

{% embed https://dev.to/chervet/why-the-hard-part-of-route-optimization-is-the-modeling-not-the-algorithm-3dc6 %}

**Why they picked it:** His very first post here, about something he's watched fail quietly for ten years: everyone benchmarks the algorithm, but most failed projects die in modeling, not solving.

**My take:** The three-layer split generalizes well beyond routing. "The rule nobody wrote down" is the same failure mode in any rules-driven system. A cookbook that maps named business rules to primitive compositions would probably close more of the gap than adding more primitives, and it would be a lot cheaper to ship.

### [Panagis Tzivras](https://dev.to/ptzivras)

{% embed https://dev.to/ptzivras/the-answer-you-didnt-want-fiskardo-evacuation-routing-4hok %}

**Why they picked it:** His evacuation-routing model confidently gave him an answer that was "geographically adventurous", and the model wasn't the only problem.

**My take:** What stuck with me is that he published the number while openly admitting one round is still unsolved. That's rare, and it makes the rest of the post far more believable than a clean ending would have. I'd love to see the actual SQL around the SRID mismatch, though.

### [Mārtiņš Veiss](https://dev.to/mrveiss)

{% embed https://dev.to/mrveiss/the-one-you-reported-is-gone-this-one-is-still-up-4pc4 %}

**Why they picked it:** It serves as a warning to the community.

**My take:** A great investigation and an important warning. Using a clean, legitimate interpreter to run a payload disguised as `cert.txt` is a clever and scary technique. With so many people installing AI skills and tools by name these days, always verify the publisher first.

### [TheBitForge](https://dev.to/thebitforge)

Read it here: [From Idea to Launch: How Developers Can Build Successful Startups](https://dev.to/thebitforge_/from-idea-to-launch-how-developers-can-build-successful-startups-50dk)

**My take:** What a gigantic post! It's packed with practical lessons, and I really liked how honest it is about the mistakes along the way. The point that the code is often the easiest part of building a startup is something every developer-founder needs to hear. Validation, pricing, and talking to customers are where most of us struggle.

### [🎩Giorgi Kobaidze](https://dev.to/georgekobaidze) (yes, that's me)

{% embed https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/metal-birds-watch-copilot-cli-helped-me-watch-planes-without-looking-up-4ha0 %}

**Why I picked it:** I built Metal Birds Watch for the GitHub Copilot CLI challenge, and it's still my biggest win. It made me dig deeper than any project before it, not just the code, but the maths and the geographic coordinate work behind it. It was an enormous amount of effort, and I was in bad shape for most of it. I'm still not sure how I got it finished, which is probably why I'm so attached to it.

---

## What I Learned From Reading All of This

**People pick their firsts.** A surprising number of you chose your very first article. Not your most polished one, not your most popular one, your first. The one you almost didn't publish. I get it, I feel the same way about mine.

**Reactions don't measure value.** Eight of these articles had zero reactions when I collected them, and several of you said yours "didn't get much interaction." Some of those were among the best things I read all month. The algorithm rewards timing, audience, and luck. It doesn't reward effort, and it doesn't reward what matters to the author.

**AI is everywhere, but the best AI posts are about where it breaks.** Rollback buttons, prompt injection tests that pass while the attack works, RAG thresholds that do nothing. The most valuable writing wasn't "look what AI can do", it was "here's what happened when I tested it properly."

**The range of this community is absurd.** Operating systems, ESP32 boards, databases built from scratch, evacuation routing on a Greek island, and a Christmas-themed legacy Java horror story. All in one thread.

---

## The Doors Will Open Again

Thank you to **every single one of you** who shared your work. Reading it was tough, but it was one of the most rewarding things I've done on DEV.

Now it's your turn. Pick at least one exhibit from this hall that you haven't read yet, and leave the author a comment. It takes two minutes and it might make someone's week.

And if you missed the first round, stay tuned, maybe there's a Vol. 2 coming. 🎩

title: I Vibe-Coded My Way Out of Angular Upgrades
author: Daniel Balcarek
body:
Do you also hate upgrading Angular versions? Because I do. I maintain a few open-source projects, and upgrading Angular is probably my least favorite maintenance task. That's also why my frontend updates often get postponed for far too long.

But we have AI now, right? It should be able to handle this with some instructions. So I decided to create (or rather vibe-code) an **Angular Update Skill for Codex**.

## Creating the skill

Upgrading Angular isn't just about running `ng update`. There are several things I normally have to take care of, so I created a prompt describing what the skill should do:

- Follow the official [Angular Update Guide](https://angular.dev/update-guide).
- Create a separate Git branch for the upgrade.
- Handle migrations and dependency updates.
- Validate that everything still builds and works.
- Follow the same good practices I would use when upgrading Angular manually.

(Updating NuGet packages in .NET feels so much simpler.)

Codex generated the first version of the skill, and surprisingly, it worked!

Well... locally.

### First problem: npm ci

After pushing my changes to GitHub, the CI pipeline failed with:

```plaintext
npm ci can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json are in sync.
```

Classic "works on my machine" problem. The skill had managed to update Angular, but it hadn't properly validated that a clean installation would work. So I added another validation step: run `npm ci` before considering the upgrade complete. This way, the agent can catch problems with the lock file before they reach CI.

### Second problem: npm publishing

Then I ran into another issue when trying to publish my Angular library to npm:

```plaintext
npm error code E404
npm error 404 Not Found - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/gramli-angular-mydatepicker - Not found
```

At first, the error wasn't particularly helpful. After some investigation, I found that my publishing environment was using Node.js 22 with npm 10.

However, according to the [npm trusted publishing documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers), trusted publishing requires:

- Node.js 22.14.0 or higher
- npm 11.5.1 or higher

So I updated the skill again to prefer the latest Node.js LTS version compatible with the target Angular version, while also making sure the npm version meets any publishing requirements.

### Third problem: the skill was getting too big

After all these improvements, the skill was becoming quite large. That might not matter much with generous token limits, but I also wanted it to be usable by people working with more limited AI budgets. So I shortened the instructions, removed unnecessary repetition, and kept the important validation steps. The main skill went from 1,252 words to 701 words, with the complete bundle becoming approximately 40% shorter.

## Testing it on real projects

Of course, generating a skill is one thing. Actually using it is another. So far, I've used the current version on three of my open-source projects:

- **Angular 21 → 22:** [angular-mydatepicker PR #12](https://github.com/Gramli/angular-mydatepicker/pull/12)
- **Angular 19 → 22:** [FileApi PR #13](https://github.com/Gramli/FileApi/pull/13)
- **Angular 21 → 22:** [AuthApi PR #113](https://github.com/Gramli/AuthApi/pull/113)

The Angular 19 → 22 upgrade was especially interesting because it required migrations across three major versions. In the AuthApi project, the upgrade also involved replacing PrimeNG with Optimus UI because of the PrimeNG licensing changes.

All three upgrades have now been merged.

## Three Projects Later

The current version works pretty well, at least on my smaller projects. It's not perfect, though. Some Angular projects are much more complicated than mine, so the skill would probably need to be adapted for them. But it already helped me upgrade three projects, and I learned a few things along the way.

The best part? I finally updated my Angular projects in just ONE WEEK instead of postponing them again. 😁

I wanted to share this with the community because it might help someone else. If you want to try the skill or improve it, you can find it here:

**[Angular Update Skill on GitHub](https://github.com/Gramli/Gramli.Framework/tree/main/src/angular-skills/angular-update)**

The npm ci failure is the part that makes this interesting. An AI agent can migrate Angular APIs correctly and still miss the contract between the lockfile, peer dependencies, and the publishing environment.

For example, in a library migrating from Angular 17 to 18, updating @angular/core and @angular/compiler-cli isn't enough if @angular-devkit/build-angular, the TypeScript version, and the library's peerDependencies still target incompatible ranges. The app may compile locally because of an existing node_modules tree, then fail in CI with a clean install or break consumers installing the published package. I'd make the skill validate those dependency constraints, run npm ci from a clean checkout, build the library in production mode, and test the packed tarball in a separate Angular consumer project. That last step catches problems a successful workspace build can easily miss.

The “improve the skill from each real failure” loop is the best part of this post, and the comments already cover clean installs, consumer testing, and regression checklists well. One angle I didn’t see yet is supply chain safety when an agent touches dependencies:
